items.title: Harry Edison — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Norman Granz called me and wanted me to make this album... Norman had told him to stand by... I got a call from Norman to do Jazz at the Philharmonic

ctx.x: His later things, he would throw in a few bars….

Sometimes he would throw it in. Like I made a record date one time out here under my name and Norman got Basie to play the piano in my band, you know, so before the date, he asked me, he says, “I’m working with you today,” I says, “Yeah”, and he says, “How much you gonna pay me?” I says, “I’m gonna pay you the same thing you been paying me, scale.” We had a big laugh. But I played something and man, he started striding…he really…I said, “Remember, my name’s on the record, not Count Basie. I don’t care how much…

items.title: 68427_Harry Edison oral history interview
items.q: He's the only one that I know that when he gives a concert, it is jazz all the way.

ctx.x: Norman Granz. He's the only one that I know that when he gives a concert, it is jazz all the way. It's all the way. I mean, it's strictly, purely culture, which is jazz music. But it belongs to the black man. And anything that belongs to the black man, there's always something to -- the white man gets something to counteract it. Because I guess, I don't know, we're all Americans, you know, and it is an American art and it's the only thing that Americans say -- America can say it is American. You can't say -- they…
But the beginning of American culture was jazz.
